title: Infra engineering consolidated guide: GPU fleet, capacity, CI/CD, IaC and runbooks
author: Ava Martinez
content:
Summary

This consolidated guide collects Redwood Inference's operational standards and runbooks for the infra engineering surface that owns the GPU fleet and capacity, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC module design, CI/CD and build pipelines, and day-to-day runbooks. It is intended for oncall engineers, SREs, platform engineers, and new members of the infra team.

Scope
- GPU fleet sizing, allocation, and autoscaling policies
- Cloud account & VPC networking patterns for production, staging, and dev
- Terraform module design, testing, and lifecycle management
- CI/CD pipeline patterns for infra changes and model-serving releases
- Runbooks for common incidents, maintenance procedures, and upgrades

Owners and contacts
- Primary owner: infra-engineering (pager: #infra-oncall)
- Secondary owner: platform-services (pager: #platform-oncall)
- Document author: Ava Martinez, Infra Engineering
- Reviewers: Lina Chen (SRE), Marcus Green (Platform), Diego Alvarez (Security)

Architecture overview
This doc assumes the following logical components: hardware GPU pool clusters (by region and tier), a control plane (Redwood control plane services), a serving runtime fleet (model worker pools), and orchestration + autoscaler components (k8s operators/cluster autoscaler or cloud autoscaling groups). Each customer environment (hosted vs dedicated vs private) maps to account/tenant boundaries described below.

1) GPU fleet and capacity planning
Purpose: ensure predictable throughput and unit economics while maintaining latency SLOs and headroom for bursty workloads.

Key metrics and targets:
- Pod/service-level SLOs: 99th-percentile tail latency targets for request scheduling and model token latency (set per-product).
- Fleet utilization target: 60-70% average GPU utilization over weekly windows.
- Headroom target: maintain 15-25% spare capacity for sudden spikes; do not schedule sustained workloads above 85% peak.
- Boot time SLO for new nodes: median boot < 6 minutes, p95 < 12 minutes.
- Queueing SLO for scheduled batches: p95 < 200 ms (scheduling queue time).

Sizing formula (example):
1. Measure p95 per-request GPU-vCPU time for the workload class (tokens/sec * time per token).
2. Desired throughput (requests/sec) = expected QPS * 1.2 (buffer factor).
3. Required gpus = ceil((desired throughput * average gpu-cost-per-request) / per-gpu-peak-requests).
4. Add 20% buffer and round up to available instance sizes.

Autoscaling and placement policies:
- Use workload classes: latency-sensitive, throughput-batch, background-async. Each has a distinct scaling policy.
- Autoscaler config defaults: min_replicas=2, scale_up_threshold=0.65, scale_down_threshold=0.25, cooldown=300s.
- Placement: prefer homogeneous clusters by model family; avoid mixing high-memory model instances with small models to reduce fragmentation.

Operational playbook (short):
1. Daily: review GPU cluster average utilization and pending queue length (dashboard: infra/gpu-cluster-overview).
2. Weekly: reconcile demand forecasts (product signals) against committed reserved capacity and adjust reservations.
3. Pre-release: for major model rollouts, provision additional on-demand capacity at least 48 hours before rollout.

2) Cloud accounts and networking
Account strategy:
- Accounts per environment: production, staging, shared-services, dev (feature envs use ephemeral accounts where possible).
- Dedicated customer accounts: provisioned per contract with network boundary and IAM isolation.

Network topology best practices:
- VPC per account with multiple AZ subnets (public/private) and transit gateway or shared VPC for cross-account services.
- Default pattern: one VPC per environment, private subnets for serving and compute, public subnets for NAT/load balancers.
- Use explicit route tables and minimal cross-AZ egress to reduce latency.

Security and observability:
- Flow logs enabled for all VPCs with 90-day retention in S3/secure logging bucket.
- Guardrails: enforce least-privilege IAM, MFA for console access, and session duration <= 12 hours for elevated roles.
- Network ACLs are avoid-listed; rely primarily on security groups and NACLs only for explicit edge controls.

Common networking recipes (examples):
- Private endpoint for control-plane services: create interface endpoints with policies limited to infra roles.
- Cross-account peering pattern: use central shared-services account and transit gateway to avoid many-to-many peering.

3) Terraform / IaC modules and conventions
Module design principles:
- Modules are small, composable, and idempotent. Each module must include inputs, outputs, and documented examples.
- Naming convention: module names use kebab-case, resources prefixed with "rwd-" to identify Redwood-managed infra.
- Versioning: modules published to the module registry and pinned in service repos with SHA or semver.

Core module inventory (representative):
- rwd-vpc (VPC + subnets + NAT + flow logs)
- rwd-eks-cluster (cluster skeleton, nodegroups, IAM roles)
- rwd-gpu-instance (GPU instance types, drivers, AMI bake integration)
- rwd-autoscaler (scaling policies, metrics, alarms)
- rwd-kms (customer-key integration for private deployments)

Module testing and lifecycle in CI:
- All module changes must include: terraform fmt, terraform validate, and unit tests with kitchen-terraform or terratest.
- Integration tests executed in ephemeral test accounts via the infra CI pipeline (see CI section).
- Module release flow: PR -> CI tests -> merge -> release tag -> module registry publish -> update dependents in a follow-up PR.

Sample usage snippet (example rwd-vpc):
```hcl
module "core_vpc" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/terraform-modules.git//rwd-vpc?ref=v0.8.3"
  name_prefix = "rwd-prod"
  cidr_block  = "10.100.0.0/16"
  az_count    = 3
  enable_flow_logs = true
}
```

4) CI/CD and build pipelines for infra
Pipeline categories:
- Module CI: validate modules, run unit tests, publish module artifact.
- Service infra pipeline: plan/apply for service repositories using locked module versions.
- Cluster ops pipeline: blue/green cluster rollout and nodegroup upgrade pipelines with canary steps.

Pipeline gates and policies:
- All terraform plan outputs must be reviewed and approved by an owner before apply.
- Changes that modify security groups, IAM, or network routes require at least 2 approvers and a security reviewer.
- Apply runs in production must be executed by a dedicated CI service account with ephemeral credentials; avoid human-run applies where possible.

Build and artifact policies:
- AMI/build images: bake images via Packer; store AMI IDs in a central artifact registry with tags indicating git commit and job.
- Container images: image signing and SBOM generation required for runtime images; scan images for critical CVEs before rollout.

Example CI pipeline steps (infra service repo):
1. Lint (tflint / tfsec)
2. Terraform init & plan against a remote workspace (non-prod)
3. Run unit & integration tests in ephemeral account
4. PR approval gates (owners + security if needed)
5. Apply in staged account -> smoke tests -> promote to prod workspace via pipeline

5) Runbooks and incident procedures
Triage and severity definitions:
- Sev1 (production-wide outage): control-plane inaccessible or serving unavailable for > 2 minutes at scale. Pager to #oncall, immediate all-hands.
- Sev2 (degraded but partial): increased error rates or latency for a subset of customers or models. Pager to relevant oncall.
- Sev3 (non-urgent): configuration or infra alarms without customer impact. Create ticket for next sprint.

Common runbooks (short excerpts):
- GPU OOM / eviction:
  1. Identify the instance and pod (dashboard: infra/gpu-pod-errors).
  2. Inspect dmesg / kernel logs for OOM killer entries.
  3. If recurring, cordon node, drain, and reprovision with larger instance type; file a postmortem if this caused customer impact.

- Node provisioning failure (pilot nodes are stuck initializing):
  1. Check instance system logs and cloud-init output (S3 or instance console).
  2. Validate driver (NVIDIA) version compatibility with AMI.
  3. Roll forward to known-good AMI if boot-time errors match regression signature.

- Network flapping / cross-region issues:
  1. Validate Transit Gateway and route tables for recent changes.
  2. Check VPC flow logs for packet rejection patterns.
  3. If due to a recent change, roll back route config and reopen a change request.

Escalation path:
- Oncall -> Senior SRE -> Platform Eng -> Director of Infra. Use the incident channel and update the status page.

Maintenance & upgrades
- Node OS/driver upgrades: schedule per-cluster with canary nodes (1-2% of fleet). Verify model correctness and perf on canaries for at least 24 hours before full rollout.
- Terraform module major version upgrades: run compatibility tests in a staging account, then coordinate cross-team dependents and run a phased rollout.

Metrics and dashboards (recommended):
- infra/gpu-cluster-overview: cluster-level GPU utilization, node counts, pending pods, pod evictions
- infra/cluster-health: nodeboot latencies, kube-api error rates, control-plane errors
- infra/network-overview: VPC bytes, rejected connections, transit gateway latencies

Appendix A — Quick checklist for new clusters
- [ ] Create account and base IAM roles (rwd-admin, rwd-deployer, rwd-audit)
- [ ] Provision VPC using rwd-vpc module with flow logs enabled
- [ ] Bake AMI with validated NVIDIA drivers and OS patches
- [ ] Provision EKS/GKE/Managed cluster with rwd-eks-cluster module
- [ ] Deploy autoscaler and monitoring agents, run canary smoke test suite

Appendix B — Example escalation runbook snippet (copyable)
1. Acknowledge pager in Slack and open incident channel: #incident-<id>
2. Assign roles: Incident Commander, Communications Lead, Tech Lead
3. Capture timeline, mitigation steps, and affected customers
4. After mitigation, schedule a postmortem within 72 hours
